text: Is the repeated line being spoken by multiple different people (rather than one person repeating it)?
Is the repeated line being spoken (or produced) by a single person or program—one entity—repeatedly?
Does a machine, device, or software program (such as a phone feature, assistant, or navigation system) produce the repeated line?
Is the repeated line from a recording or a written/printed text (not a machine's synthesized speech)?
Is the repeated line a recording played back through a speaker (such as a voicemail, answering machine, or automated recording)?
Is the repeated line a written/printed text repeated many times (such as being written over and over on paper or a wall)?
Is the written repeated line addressed specifically to the narrator (i.e., the narrator is the "you" being addressed)?
Is the repeated written line found in a book or printed story (rather than handwritten by a character)?
Was the repeated line handwritten by a character in the story?
Does the narrative concern a death (someone has died or will die)?
Did the writer of the repeated line die (i.e., is it a suicide note or a note left before dying)?
Did the narrator cause (or believe they caused) the death?
Is the death a suicide of someone the narrator hurt (narrator drove the person to suicide)?
Was the death an accident caused by the narrator's negligence (rather than intentional killing)?
Did the narrator intentionally kill the person who died?
Did the narrator murder the person who wrote the repeated line's loved one (i.e., the writer is a bereaved relative/partner of the murder victim)?
Is the note-writer a parent or guardian of the narrator?
Does the narrator personally know the person who died (they had a prior relationship)?
Is the person who died the note-writer's romantic partner or spouse?
Were the narrator and the note-writer romantically involved with each other?
Did the note-writer discover that the narrator had killed the writer's spouse, and leave the narrator forever as a result?
Did the note-writer know that the narrator had killed the note-writer's spouse?
Was the repeated line originally written by the note-writer to address their own (now-deceased) spouse, rather than composed for the narrator?
Did the note-writer leave the narrator for a reason unrelated to the narrator's crime (so the "disappointment" is about something else, like romance/behavior)?

Is the "disappointment" and departure actually about the narrator's crime—even though the note-writer doesn't know it was the narrator who killed the spouse (e.g., the writer leaves because the narrator seemed to fail/be involved in the spouse's death)?
Did the note-writer leave/stop seeing the narrator *before* the spouse's death occurred?
Was the repeated line written by the note-writer as a public/multiple-copy message — e.g., posted around (on walls, notes, social media) to shame or reject the narrator?
Is the repeated writing something like a diary/journal entry or letter where the writer kept repeating the same line out of emotional distress?
Does the note-writer believe the spouse's death was something other than a deliberate murder (e.g., an accident, illness, or natural death)?
Did the note-writer know the spouse was murdered (by someone), even if not knowing the narrator was the killer?
Did the note-writer suspect or accuse the narrator of the murder (believing the narrator was involved), even without certain knowledge?
Was the handwritten note left for the narrator to find as a farewell when the note-writer departed?
Is the repeated line something the note-writer was made to write as a punishment or task (like "write lines" repeatedly)?
Is the narrator a child or young person relative to the note-writer?
Is the narrator the police detective investigating the spouse's murder (i.e., the narrator is not the killer in this reading)?

Is the "death" actually the murder of the narrator's rival/romantic partner by someone else—i.e., did I over-attribute the killing to the narrator? (Please answer whether the narrator personally caused the death.)
Is the note-writer a different person from the narrator (not the same individual)?
Is the narrator a prisoner or someone confined who writes the line repeatedly in a cell or enclosed space?

Did the host's earlier "yes" to "narrator and note-writer were romantically involved" actually apply to a different pair than narrator-and-writer (given writer=narrator)? Please answer: was the narrator romantically involved with the person they killed?
At the time the narrator wrote the line 7 times, was the person the narrator loved (whom the narrator killed) already dead?
Before being killed, did that person say or write this same line to the narrator as a rejection or departure ("I'm never coming back")?
Does "I'm never coming back" in the repeated line refer to the dead person never returning because they are dead (death itself is the "not coming back")?
Does the repeated line reflect something the narrator is writing about themselves — i.e., the narrator is the one who is "disappointed" and "never coming back" (the narrator plans to leave or die)?
Is the narrator writing the line over and over in order to practice or forge the handwriting (or voice) of the person they killed — e.g., to fake a note that the victim left?

The narrator murdered the person they loved—their own spouse/partner. To conceal the killing, the narrator set about forging a farewell note in the victim's handwriting, making it appear the victim had walked out and simply left forever ("I'm never coming back"). As forged evidence of the abandonment, the narrator obsessively handwrote the victim's supposed parting words—"You've disappointed me so much; I'm never coming back"—again and again, practicing the handwriting so the fake note would pass as the dead spouse's own writing (which is why a single hand wrote the line repeatedly, why the phrase is simultaneously "addressed to the narrator" and not, and why it is not a real farewell/rejection actually voiced by the victim). The line is not machine or recorded speech, nor found in a book; it is the murderer's handwritten forgery rehearsal. Looking at the repeated practice copies, the narrator sighs, "I know I'm in trouble"—because the incriminating forgeries will expose the murder and the lie that the spouse left of their own accord.
Does the repeated handwritten line represent the narrator practicing to *frame or imitate the writing of a different person than the one they killed* (e.g., to forge someone else's note)?
Is the narrator writing the line to imitate the handwriting of the person they killed—so that a "goodbye, I'm leaving you" note would seem to be genuinely written by that victim?
Was the person the narrator killed actually married to the narrator (their own spouse)?
Does "Sigh, I know I'm in trouble" mean the narrator knows they will be caught or punished for the murder/forgery (rather than referring to grief or to the dead spouse)?
Is the specific reason the narrator writes the same line 7 times that each repetition is one practice attempt—i.e., the copies are drafts, not the display of a finished fake note?

The narrator deliberately murdered their own spouse. To conceal the murder, the narrator needed it to look as though the spouse had not been killed but had instead walked out and left the narrator for good—so the narrator set out to forge a farewell note in the dead spouse's handwriting. The repeated identical line, "You've disappointed me so much; I'm never coming back," is the text of that fake abandonment note, and the many copies are the narrator's practice drafts: the narrator handwrote the same sentence over and over to rehearse/imitate the dead spouse's handwriting well enough that the forged "I'm leaving you and never coming back" note would pass as genuinely written by the victim. It is one hand writing repeatedly (not several speakers, not a machine or recording, not a printed book), and this is why the line is both "addressed to the narrator" (it is a message from the spouse to the narrator) and not (the narrator is only fabricating it). Looking at the failed practice copies, the narrator sighs, "I know I'm in trouble"—realizing these incriminating forgeries will expose the murder and the lie that the spouse simply left.
